patient.name: Sunil Mehta
patient.complaint: Routine annual diabetes check; feels well
background: Type 2 diabetes for 14 years, on metformin and gliclazide
HbA1c has drifted up over two years

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis/cause?' in a long-standing diabetic with a raised ACR, or oedema with heavy proteinuria and a normal echo. Retinopathy in the stem is a strong pointer.

points: Here for his annual review; **no symptoms at all**.
BP has been running in the 140s.
HbA1c has crept up from 53 to 64 mmol/mol.

steps.lead: Years of **hyperglycaemia** quietly damage Sunil's glomeruli long before he notices anything.
Sunil has every risk factor: diabetes, **hypertension**, **poor control** and a **long duration**.

steps.title: Annual review bloods and urine
steps.text: Only the ACR is clearly abnormal. That is exactly what early disease looks like.

visual.title: Urine albumin:creatinine ratio
visual.label: Sunil 9
visual.caption: Sunil sits in the **microalbuminuria** band (3 to 30): the first sign of diabetic nephropathy.

steps.lead: Sunil is asymptomatic with **microalbuminuria only**: the earliest stage on the road to CKD.

steps.title: How it progresses
steps.caption: Catching it at the microalbuminuria step is the whole point of screening.

steps.q: Sunil feels well but his ACR is 9 mg/mmol. What is the earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy?
steps.r: **Microalbuminuria** comes first. Oedema and low albumin are late features of heavy proteinuria.

steps.lead: If Sunil's disease progresses, protein loss gives **oedema** and **low albumin**; his biggest risk is **cardiovascular disease**.

steps.text: Blood on dipstick or a rapid fall in eGFR is **not** typical of diabetic nephropathy. Think glomerulonephritis or another cause.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is an early morning urine ACR, and questions on how persistent albuminuria is confirmed (2 of 3 readings over 3 months).

steps.q: Which test screens every diabetic patient for nephropathy each year?
steps.r: **Early morning urine ACR** picks up microalbuminuria that a dipstick misses.

steps.lead: Sunil's annual **early morning ACR** caught it; his eGFR, U&Es, lipids and HbA1c complete the picture.

points: Sunil repeats the early morning ACR twice over 3 months.
Three raised readings: persistent, not a one-off.

visual.title: Sunil's confirmation ACRs
visual.caption: All above 3 mg/mmol: at least **2 of 3 elevated over 3 months** confirms it.

steps.lead: Sunil now meets the gold standard: a **persistently elevated ACR**, confirmed on 2 of 3 readings over at least 3 months.

steps.text: A single raised ACR does not make the diagnosis. Infection, exercise and menstruation can raise it transiently, so **repeat** it.

steps.lead: Sunil will now have **ACR and eGFR** checked regularly to track severity.

steps.text: ACR thresholds: **≥3 mg/mmol** = microalbuminuria, **≥30 mg/mmol** = macroalbuminuria. The same 3 also triggers an ACE inhibitor.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate medication?' in a diabetic with a raised ACR: ACE inhibitor or ARB first, then SGLT2 inhibitor if ACR >30 in type 2, and indapamide for BP still high.

steps.q: Sunil's ACR is persistently 9 mg/mmol and his BP 146/88. What should be started?
steps.r: An **ACE inhibitor** (ramipril) or ARB is indicated for ACR ≥3: it lowers BP and reduces proteinuria.

steps.lead: Sunil starts **ramipril**, titrated up, aiming for BP **130/80 mmHg** and a better HbA1c.

points: Two years later his ACR has risen to **42 mg/mmol**.

steps.lead: Type 2, CKD, on an ACE inhibitor, ACR >30: Sunil adds **dapagliflozin**. If BP stayed high, **indapamide** would be next.

steps.title: Drug ladder
nodes: ACR ≥3 mg/mmol → ACE inhibitor or ARB
BP still high → add thiazide-like diuretic

visual.title: Sunil's ACR on treatment
visual.caption: Each step reduces albuminuria, which slows CKD progression.

steps.lead: Sunil's ACR is not above 70, but **<130/80** is still the target; he gets **statin**, salt reduction and weight advice.

steps.text: Never combine an ACE inhibitor **and** an ARB. Check potassium and creatinine 1 to 2 weeks after starting or increasing either.

steps.lead: Had Sunil's potassium climbed with a falling eGFR, that signals advanced disease: **urgent nephrology**.
If Sunil reaches advanced CKD, **nephrology** plans for **dialysis or transplant**.
Sunil's care follows **NICE NG28 and NG203**, plus KDIGO for CKD.

steps.text: Watch for **vaginal or genital candidiasis** with SGLT2 inhibitors; it is the classic side effect the exam asks about.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why ACE inhibitors reduce proteinuria (efferent dilation), how SGLT2 inhibitors work (tubuloglomerular feedback), or the classic biopsy finding (Kimmelstiel-Wilson).

steps.lead: Sunil's glomeruli first **hyperfilter**, then the basement membrane thickens and podocytes fail, so albumin leaks out.

steps.q: Which histological finding is classic of advanced diabetic nephropathy?
steps.r: **Nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson)** is the classic finding. Crescents suggest rapidly progressive GN.

steps.lead: Ramipril **dilates Sunil's efferent arteriole**; dapagliflozin **constricts his afferent** one. Both lower intraglomerular pressure.

steps.text: A small creatinine rise (under about 30%) after starting an ACE inhibitor is expected: it reflects the lower glomerular pressure.

mcq.q: What is the first sign of diabetic nephropathy?
mcq.r: **Microalbuminuria** is the first sign; it is often asymptomatic.

mcq.q: Which is a late feature of diabetic nephropathy?
mcq.r: Heavy protein loss gives **low albumin**, oedema and ascites with a low SAAG (<1.1 g/dL).

mcq.q: Which is the commonest serious complication of diabetic nephropathy?
mcq.r: **Cardiovascular disease** is a major complication, alongside CKD and end-stage renal failure.

o: 2 of 3 raised ACRs over at least 3 months
mcq.r: **2 of 3 elevated readings over at least 3 months**.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for a diabetic with ACR ≥3 mg/mmol?
mcq.r: An **ACE inhibitor (e.g. ramipril) or ARB** reduces proteinuria and BP.

mcq.q: Which side effect is typical of dapagliflozin?
mcq.r: Glycosuria from **SGLT2 inhibitors** predisposes to **genital candidiasis**.

mcq.q: What is the BP target in CKD with ACR >70 mg/mmol?
mcq.r: **<130/80 mmHg** when there is significant proteinuria.

mcq.q: How do ACE inhibitors reduce proteinuria?
mcq.r: **Efferent dilation** lowers intraglomerular pressure and protein leak.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman with type 1 diabetes for 20 years attends clinic. She has background diabetic retinopathy. She feels well. Her HbA1c has been above 70 mmol/mol for several years. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/90 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows protein 2+ and no blood.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about proteinuria in a diabetic: ask whether diabetes explains it all.
Long duration, poor control, hypertension and another **microvascular** complication; protein without blood.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ACR 45 = **macroalbuminuria** in a long-standing, poorly controlled diabetic with retinopathy: **diabetic nephropathy**.

elim: IgA nephropathy gives **visible haematuria** after a sore throat; there is no blood.
Minimal change gives sudden heavy nephrotic syndrome, usually in children.
PKD has a family history, flank pain and haematuria.
Renal artery stenosis gives resistant hypertension and creatinine rise on ACE inhibitor, not heavy albuminuria.

steps.x: **A. Diabetic nephropathy.** Rule: retinopathy + long diabetes + albuminuria without blood = diabetic nephropathy.

technique.stem: A 57 year old man with type 2 diabetes has a urine albumin:creatinine ratio of 6 mg/mmol at his annual review. He has no urinary symptoms. His previous ACR a year ago was normal. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

steps.x: The next investigation after one raised ACR: you need to prove it is **persistent**.

clues: previous ACR a year ago was normal
steps.x: A first raised ACR in the microalbuminuria range, with no infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm with **repeat early morning ACRs**: 2 of 3 raised over at least 3 months.

elim: 24-hour collections are cumbersome; ACR is the test used.
Biopsy is only for atypical features such as haematuria or rapid decline.
Ultrasound does not show albuminuria.
The dipstick shows no infection.

steps.x: **D. Repeat early morning urine ACR.** Rule: one raised ACR is a flag; 2 of 3 over 3 months is a diagnosis.

technique.stem: A 66 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease takes metformin and ramipril 10 mg daily. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. She has no history of ketoacidosis.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate additional medication?

steps.x: An add-on drug for someone already on an ACE inhibitor: what does her ACR and BP tell you?
Type 2, CKD, on maximum ACE inhibitor, **ACR >30**, BP already at target.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Add an **SGLT2 inhibitor**: dapagliflozin.

elim: Her BP is at target; amlodipine does not reduce albuminuria.
Never combine an ARB with an ACE inhibitor.
She is not fluid overloaded.
Indapamide is for BP above target on a maximised ACE inhibitor; hers is controlled.

steps.x: **C. Dapagliflozin.** Rule: type 2 + CKD + ACE inhibitor + ACR >30 = add SGLT2 inhibitor.

technique.stem: A 59 year old man with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria is started on dapagliflozin. Six months later his urine albumin:creatinine ratio has fallen from 40 to 24 mg/mmol.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the reduction in albuminuria?
o: Afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction via tubuloglomerular feedback
Efferent arteriolar vasodilation via reduced angiotensin II

steps.x: A mechanism question about the SGLT2 inhibitor specifically.
SGLT2 blocks sodium-glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: More sodium reaches the **macula densa** → **afferent** constriction → lower glomerular pressure.

elim: Efferent dilation is how **ACE inhibitors/ARBs** work.
Podocytes do not regenerate with this drug.
Aldosterone reduction is not its main renal effect.
It does not act through sympathetic nerves.

steps.x: **A. Afferent vasoconstriction via tubuloglomerular feedback.** Rule: ACE inhibitor = efferent; SGLT2 = afferent.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman with type 2 diabetes for 25 years has a 3 month history of bilateral ankle swelling. She has diabetic retinopathy. She is not breathless. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 152/86 mmHg. There is pitting oedema to the knees. Echocardiogram shows normal systolic function. Urinalysis shows protein 3+ and no blood, nitrites or leucocytes.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her peripheral oedema?
practice.e: Long-standing diabetes with retinopathy, heavy proteinuria without blood and low albumin is diabetic nephropathy. The normal echo excludes cardiac failure.

steps.x: A cause of oedema question: cardiac, renal or lymphatic?
Heart is fine; heavy proteinuria with low albumin in a long-standing diabetic with retinopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Late diabetic nephropathy causing hypoalbuminaemia and **oedema**.

elim: Amyloidosis is possible but needs a cause like myeloma or chronic inflammation; diabetes explains it.
Normal echo and no breathlessness.
GN gives **blood** in the urine; there is none.
Lymphoedema does not cause proteinuria or low albumin.

steps.x: **C. Diabetic nephropathy.** Rule: diabetic + retinopathy + protein without blood + normal echo.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 9 years attends his annual review. He has no symptoms. His BMI is 33 kg/m². His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 142/88 mmHg. Three early morning urine samples over 4 months show raised albumin:creatinine ratios. Urine dipstick shows no blood.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Persistent microalbuminuria (ACR 3 to 30) on repeated early morning samples in an asymptomatic diabetic is early diabetic nephropathy. Orthostatic proteinuria is excluded by early morning samples.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an asymptomatic diabetic with an abnormal urine test.

clues: Three early morning urine samples over 4 months
steps.x: Persistent ACR 3 to 30 = **microalbuminuria**; confirmed over 3 months.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Early **diabetic nephropathy**.

elim: AIN follows a new drug, with rash, fever and an acute creatinine rise.
IgA nephropathy causes haematuria.
Orthostatic proteinuria is absent in **early morning** samples.
UTI gives symptoms and a positive dipstick.

steps.x: **B. Diabetic nephropathy.** Rule: persistent ACR ≥3 in a diabetic is diabetic nephropathy until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has had type 1 diabetes for 12 years. She is asymptomatic. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Her GP is concerned she is developing diabetic kidney disease and wants to look for the earliest detectable abnormality.
practice.q: Which is the most likely first abnormal finding?
practice.e: Microalbuminuria is the first sign of diabetic nephropathy, appearing years before creatinine rises. Oedema and low albumin are late features.

steps.x: The **earliest** abnormality: think of the first stage of the disease.
Asymptomatic: early disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Microalbuminuria** (ACR ≥3 mg/mmol).

elim: Hyperkalaemia comes with advanced CKD.
Low albumin needs heavy protein loss: late.
Oedema is a late feature.
Creatinine rises only after substantial nephron loss.

steps.x: **C. Microalbuminuria.** Rule: first sign = microalbuminuria; that is why ACR is screened yearly.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 22 years has a renal biopsy because his proteinuria is heavier than expected. He has diabetic retinopathy. Light microscopy shows a thickened glomerular basement membrane, mesangial expansion and rounded acellular nodules within the glomeruli.
practice.q: Which is the most likely histological diagnosis?
practice.e: Rounded mesangial nodules with GBM thickening in a long-standing diabetic are Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions: nodular glomerulosclerosis, the classic finding in advanced diabetic nephropathy.

steps.x: Name the histological finding.

clues: thickened glomerular basement membrane, mesangial expansion
steps.x: The three classic diabetic changes, ending in **nodules**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Kimmelstiel-Wilson** nodular glomerulosclerosis.

elim: Crescents mean rapidly progressive GN.
FSGS shows segmental scarring, not nodules.
Membranous shows subepithelial spikes, not nodules.
IgA deposits are seen on immunofluorescence, with haematuria.

steps.x: **E. Nodular glomerulosclerosis.** Rule: diabetic + nodules = Kimmelstiel-Wilson.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with type 2 diabetes and known heavy proteinuria has a 2 month history of increasing abdominal swelling and ankle oedema. He drinks no alcohol. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 150/90 mmHg. There is shifting dullness and pitting oedema. There are no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Ascitic tap is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his ascites?
practice.e: A low SAAG (<1.1 g/dL) means the ascites is not from portal hypertension; with heavy proteinuria and low albumin it is from diabetic nephropathy. Cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari, heart failure and portal vein thrombosis give a high SAAG.

steps.x: Cause of ascites: start with the **SAAG**.

clues: no stigmata of chronic liver disease
steps.x: SAAG <1.1 = **not** portal hypertension; very low serum albumin from protein loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Late **diabetic nephropathy** with hypoalbuminaemia.

elim: Cirrhosis gives a high SAAG; no alcohol or liver stigmata.
Budd-Chiari gives a high SAAG with painful hepatomegaly.
Heart failure gives a high SAAG.
Portal vein thrombosis gives a high SAAG.

steps.x: **D. Diabetic nephropathy.** Rule: low SAAG + heavy proteinuria in a diabetic = renal protein loss.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has diabetic nephropathy with macroalbuminuria and an eGFR of 41 mL/min/1.73m². She asks what her greatest long-term risk is. She has hypertension and takes ramipril and atorvastatin. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of death in this patient?
practice.e: Albuminuria and CKD in diabetes greatly raise cardiovascular risk; most patients die of cardiovascular disease before reaching end-stage renal failure.

steps.x: The commonest cause of death, not the commonest renal outcome.
Albuminuria is a powerful **cardiovascular** risk marker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cardiovascular disease** (MI, stroke).

elim: DKA is a type 1 emergency, not the usual death here.
Hyperkalaemia is a risk in advanced CKD, but less common.
Not linked to diabetic nephropathy.
Uraemia occurs only in untreated end-stage disease.

steps.x: **A. Cardiovascular disease.** Rule: in diabetic kidney disease, the heart usually fails before the kidneys do.

practice.stem: A 49 year old man is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. He has no urinary symptoms. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. The practice nurse is setting up his annual checks to detect kidney complications as early as possible.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate screening investigation?
practice.e: All diabetic patients have an annual early morning urine ACR, which detects microalbuminuria earlier than a dipstick or PCR.

steps.x: A **screening** test for diabetic kidney disease.
Earliest detection = microalbuminuria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Annual **early morning urine ACR**.

elim: Ultrasound does not detect early disease.
Cystatin C estimates GFR, which falls late.
Dipstick misses microalbuminuria.
PCR is less sensitive than ACR for small amounts of albumin.

steps.x: **A. Early morning urine ACR.** Rule: diabetic + screening for kidney damage = ACR every year.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with type 2 diabetes has persistent microalbuminuria confirmed on three early morning samples. His GP now wants to stage his chronic kidney disease. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 140/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which additional investigation is most appropriate?
practice.e: CKD is staged by eGFR (from serum creatinine) plus ACR; together they are used for ongoing monitoring. Biopsy is reserved for atypical features.

steps.x: He already has the ACR; what else stages CKD?
Staging uses **ACR plus eGFR**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **U&Es with eGFR**.

elim: Biopsy only if atypical (haematuria, rapid decline).
Ultrasound is for obstruction or unexplained CKD.
Albumin is low only in late heavy proteinuria.

steps.x: **D. Serum creatinine with eGFR.** Rule: CKD = eGFR category + ACR category.

practice.stem: A 55 year old woman with type 2 diabetes takes metformin and atorvastatin. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 144/88 mmHg. Repeat early morning urine samples confirm persistent albuminuria. She is not pregnant and has no drug allergies.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate medication to prescribe?
practice.e: ACR ≥3 mg/mmol in diabetes is the indication for an ACE inhibitor or ARB, which reduces proteinuria as well as BP. Amlodipine lowers BP but does not protect the kidney in the same way.

steps.x: A first drug in a diabetic with albuminuria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: CCBs do not reduce proteinuria like RAAS blockade.
A thiazide comes later, if BP stays high on an ACE inhibitor.
Alpha-blockers are late add-ons.
Spironolactone is not first-line and raises potassium.

steps.x: **D. Lisinopril.** Rule: diabetic + ACR ≥3 = ACE inhibitor or ARB, regardless of age or ethnicity.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy takes metformin and the maximum dose of ramipril. He is already taking dapagliflozin. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 148/90 mmHg on repeated readings. He has no oedema.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Suboptimal BP despite a maximised ACE inhibitor in CKD calls for a thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide. Adding an ARB to an ACE inhibitor is not recommended.

steps.x: Next step with BP still above target.
RAAS blockade maximised; BP above 130/80.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Add a **thiazide-like diuretic**: indapamide.

elim: Never combine ACE inhibitor and ARB.
Loop diuretics are for fluid overload; he has none.
Ramipril is already at maximum dose.
Dapagliflozin is protecting his kidneys; there is no reason to stop it.

steps.x: **C. Add indapamide.** Rule: BP high on max ACE inhibitor in CKD = thiazide-like diuretic.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy takes ramipril and dapagliflozin. Over 6 months her eGFR has fallen from 32 to 17 mL/min/1.73m². She feels tired. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. ECG shows no acute changes.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Worsening renal function with high potassium in a diabetic suggests advanced disease and needs urgent nephrology input, including planning for dialysis or transplant.

steps.x: Next step in a deteriorating patient.
Rapidly falling eGFR plus **hyperkalaemia** = advanced disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent nephrology** referral.

elim: BP is near target; amlodipine does not address the problem.
Spironolactone would raise potassium further.
More ramipril would worsen hyperkalaemia.
Six months is far too long with this decline.

steps.x: **D. Refer urgently to nephrology.** Rule: rising potassium + falling eGFR in a diabetic = urgent nephrology.

practice.stem: A 56 year old man with type 2 diabetes and an albumin:creatinine ratio of 18 mg/mmol starts ramipril. Three months later his ACR has fallen to 7 mg/mmol and his creatinine has risen by 12%. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the fall in albuminuria?
practice.e: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II, dilating the efferent arteriole and lowering intraglomerular pressure, so less albumin leaks. The small creatinine rise reflects that lower pressure.

steps.x: Mechanism of an ACE inhibitor on the glomerulus.
Less albumin and a little less filtration: glomerular pressure has fallen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Angiotensin II normally constricts the **efferent** arteriole; blocking it **dilates** it.

elim: Afferent constriction is the SGLT2 inhibitor mechanism.
GFR falls slightly, as the creatinine shows.
Tubular reabsorption is not how it works.
Matrix change is slow and not the immediate effect.

steps.x: **B. Efferent arteriolar vasodilation.** Rule: ACE inhibitor = efferent dilation = lower intraglomerular pressure.

glossary.ACR: Urine albumin:creatinine ratio; a spot urine test for albumin leakage, corrected for urine concentration.
glossary.Microalbuminuria: Small amounts of albumin in the urine (ACR 3 to 30 mg/mmol); the first sign of diabetic nephropathy.
glossary.Macroalbuminuria: Larger albumin leak (ACR 30 mg/mmol or more); overt proteinuria.
glossary.Proteinuria: Protein in the urine, showing the glomerular filter is leaking.
glossary.eGFR: Estimated glomerular filtration rate; calculated from serum creatinine to stage kidney function.
glossary.CKD: Chronic kidney disease: reduced kidney function or kidney damage lasting more than 3 months.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes blood test: sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine.
glossary.HbA1c: Glycated haemoglobin; reflects average blood glucose over about 3 months.
glossary.SAAG: Serum-ascites albumin gradient; 1.1 g/dL or more suggests portal hypertension, below suggests other causes like protein loss.
glossary.Hypoalbuminaemia: Low blood albumin, causing fluid to leak into tissues as oedema.
glossary.Ascites: Fluid collecting in the peritoneal cavity, causing abdominal swelling.
glossary.Oedema: Swelling from fluid in the tissues, often pitting at the ankles.
glossary.Glomerular hyperfiltration: Abnormally high filtration per glomerulus; the earliest change in diabetic kidneys.
glossary.GBM: Glomerular basement membrane; the filter layer between capillary and Bowman's space.
glossary.Mesangial expansion: Increase in the supporting matrix between glomerular capillaries.
glossary.Podocyte: Specialised cell wrapping glomerular capillaries whose foot processes stop protein leaking.
glossary.Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions: Rounded nodules of nodular glomerulosclerosis; the classic biopsy finding of advanced diabetic nephropathy.
glossary.Nodular glomerulosclerosis: Scarring of glomeruli into rounded nodules; same as Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions.
glossary.RAAS: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system; hormone cascade that raises BP and constricts the efferent arteriole.
glossary.Efferent arteriole: Vessel carrying blood out of the glomerulus; dilating it lowers glomerular pressure.
glossary.Afferent arteriole: Vessel carrying blood into the glomerulus; constricting it lowers glomerular pressure.
glossary.Macula densa: Sodium-sensing cells in the distal tubule that signal the afferent arteriole.
glossary.Tubuloglomerular feedback: Reflex where more sodium at the macula densa constricts the afferent arteriole.
glossary.ACE inhibitor: Drug (e.g. ramipril) that blocks angiotensin II production, lowering BP and proteinuria.
glossary.ARB: Angiotensin receptor blocker (e.g. losartan); an alternative to an ACE inhibitor.
glossary.Ramipril: ACE inhibitor used first-line for diabetic nephropathy with ACR 3 mg/mmol or more.
glossary.SGLT2 inhibitor: Drug (e.g. dapagliflozin) blocking glucose and sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
glossary.Dapagliflozin: SGLT2 inhibitor that slows CKD progression; can cause genital candidiasis.
glossary.Indapamide: Thiazide-like diuretic added when BP stays high despite a maximised ACE inhibitor or ARB.
glossary.Vaginal candidiasis: Thrush; a common side effect of SGLT2 inhibitors due to glucose in the urine.
glossary.Retinopathy: Diabetic damage to retinal vessels; its presence supports diabetic nephropathy as the cause of proteinuria.
glossary.Glomerulonephritis: Inflammation of the glomeruli, usually with blood and protein in the urine.
glossary.IgA nephropathy: Glomerulonephritis with IgA deposits, typically visible haematuria after a sore throat.
glossary.Dialysis: Artificial removal of waste and fluid from the blood when the kidneys fail.
glossary.End-stage renal failure: Kidney function too low to sustain life without dialysis or transplant.
glossary.KDIGO: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes; international guideline body for kidney disease.
glossary.Hyperkalaemia: High blood potassium; a danger in advanced CKD and with ACE inhibitors.
